### Observed differences

- Across six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22), the resources carrying out the work changed almost completely. In the earlier window, User_37 was the largest named handler (about 10–11 assignments in 100) and User_39 the next (about 7–9 in 100); in the later window neither appears among the top resources of any of these activities, and a largely different set of resources took over, each with roughly 3–9 assignments in 100. The diffuse remainder stayed at about 40–55 assignments in 100 in both windows. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A13 and A14 show identical before/after profiles, so they most likely reflect one shared allocation behaviour rather than two independent changes. [ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]
- A11 moved from shared to single-resource handling: earlier it was spread across 18 distinct resources with the top one taking about 18 assignments in 100 (concentration index about 0.10); in the later window every observed assignment went to one resource, User_115 (top share 100 in 100, concentration index 1.0). [ASSIGN003, CONC001]
- Participation did not change: the observation volumes behind each profile are similar across windows (for example A01 with 200 vs 200, A11 with 107 vs 101, A17 with 246 vs 250), so the difference is who performed the activities, not how often the activities occurred. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN006]
- Every flagged difference is larger than what appeared in about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the process's resource allocation changed. Main hypothesis: work on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reassigned from one group of resources, previously led by User_37 and User_39, to a largely different group, while activity A11, previously shared across 18 resources, became handled exclusively by User_115. Supporting signs: the resource family produced 8 qualifying items where fewer than 0.01 would be expected if nothing had changed — a count many times the chance expectation, which random splitting cannot explain as a whole; all items point in the same direction (redistribution); the same resources decline and a common new set rises across all six activities; and stable observation volumes argue against a shift in activity frequency. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles, teams or mechanisms (routing rule versus roster change) can be inferred, and because the items likely express one underlying reassignment they are not independent confirmations. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is that the two windows simply sample different natural staffing periods; the cross-activity consistency makes pure sampling fluctuation unlikely, but a gradual rotation outside the observed windows cannot be excluded.

Other differences: none are reported — the control-flow and time families produced no qualifying items (0 against about 0.17 and 0.02 expected by chance), so no structural or timing difference is indicated at these thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]
